I read the test and the implementation. The test passes `source_text = r"A_B[C](D)~E\`F>G#H+I-J=K|L{M}.N! and slash \\\\ end"` and calls `escape_markdown(source_text, version=2)` with no `entity_type`.

In `telegram/helpers.py`, `escape_markdown` checks `version`. Since `int(version) == 2`, it enters the `elif` block. Because `entity_type` is omitted, it is `None`, so it is neither in `["pre", "code"]` nor in `["text_link", "custom_emoji"]`. Therefore the `else` branch at lines 72-73 sets:

`escape_chars = r"\_*[]()~`>#+-=|{}.!"`

Then line 77 does:
`re.sub(f"([{re.escape(escape_chars)}])", r"\\\1", text)`

So every occurrence in the input text of any character from that set gets prefixed with a backslash. Applying that to the given text:
- `_` → `\_`
- `[` → `\[`
- `]` → `\]`
- `(` → `\(`
- `)` → `\)`
- `~` → `\~`
- `` ` `` → `\``
- `>` → `\>`
- `#` → `\#`
- `+` → `\+`
- `-` → `\-`
- `=` → `\=`
- `|` → `\|`
- `{` → `\{`
- `}` → `\}`
- `.` → `\.`
- `!` → `\!`

The input also already contains two literal backslashes before ` end` because the test uses a raw string with `\\\\`. Since backslash itself is included in `escape_chars`, each of those two backslashes is escaped by adding another backslash before it, producing four backslashes in the returned Python string at that position.

So the returned string is:
`A\_B\[C\]\(D\)\~E\`F\>G\#H\+I\-J\=K\|L\{M\}\.N\! and slash \\\\ end`
